title: Vokes v. Arthur Murray, Inc.
summary: An allegedly deceptive campaign by expert dance instructors could support rescission even though their assurances were framed as opinions about ability and progress.

sections.Parties: Audrey Vokes sued the dance-school operator and Arthur Murray, Inc. over the purchase of repeated courses of dance lessons.
sections.Material Facts:
Vokes was a 51-year-old widow without family who hoped to become an accomplished dancer and find a new interest. She first bought eight half-hour lessons for $14.50 after a dance party and an intensive sales presentation. Within less than sixteen months she purchased fourteen courses totaling 2,302 hours for $31,090.45. Additional courses were sold while hundreds of previously purchased hours remained unused.

Her complaint alleged persistent praise of her grace, improvement, and potential; aptitude tests that purported to identify the further instruction needed; and promises of eligibility for medals. It also alleged that the instructors knew she was not improving, had no dance aptitude, and had difficulty hearing the musical beat. She claimed the assurances were deliberately false and induced the additional purchases.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice for failure to state a cause of action. The Florida appellate court reversed. It accepted the material allegations as true for that pleading-stage decision and allowed Vokes to proceed; it did not find after trial that the allegations were proved or enter a final rescission award.
sections.Issue: Could the alleged statements and sales methods support relief despite the usual distinction between misrepresentations of fact and expressions of opinion?
sections.Holding: Yes. The allegations of superior knowledge, deceptive methods, and unequal access to the truth were sufficient to permit the action.
sections.Reasoning:
The general protection for opinions has qualifications. A representation made by a party with superior knowledge may reasonably be treated as a factual assurance when the parties do not deal on equal informational terms. The dance instructors could assess aptitude and progress in ways Vokes could not. The alleged testing and repeated assurances accordingly had significance beyond casual compliments.

The complaint also described an organized pattern of inducement: expensive additional instruction, large unused balances, and statements knowingly inconsistent with actual progress. Once the instructors undertook to explain her progress, they could not withhold facts necessary to make that account truthful. On those allegations the court could not treat the entire transaction as permissible sales praise between parties bargaining at arm’s length.

The decision gives Vokes an opportunity to prove the claim. Its rhetoric about unfairness does not eliminate that procedural limitation. The editors question the court’s characterization of the transaction and discuss later legislative regulation separately.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It demonstrates how the speaker’s expertise and the surrounding sales process can change the legal significance of apparently subjective praise.

topics.misrepresentation: Expert assurances and deceptive sales methods could support relief.
topics.assent: The complaint alleged that false assessments induced repeated purchases.
topics.disclosure: An undertaken account of progress had to include the material truth.
topics.discretion: Evaluative judgment does not give an expert seller unrestricted permission to deceive.

mnemonic.rationale: Fourteen hundred hours of dance lessons
